question: What is the recommended carbohydrate intake per hour during prolonged intermittent sports lasting 1 to 2 hours according to the review on acute effects of carbohydrate supplementation?

Drawing on energy system demands that rely heavily on muscle glycogen and blood glucose, the review finds that carbohydrate ingestion generally enhances high-intensity running capacity, delays fatigue, and helps maintain sport-specific technical skills towards the end of prolonged play. Based on these findings, the paper recommends carbohydrate intake during prolonged intermittent exertion to preserve plasma glucose oxidation and central nervous system function, providing guidelines that favor consuming 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour—or utilizing carbohydrate mouth rinsing for shorter high-intensity sessions—to optimize overall athletic performance.
passage_2: Personalized Approach for the Management of Exercise-Related Glycemic Imbalances in Type 1 Diabetes: Comparison with Reference Method evaluates the efficacy of the personalized Exercise Carbohydrate Requirement Estimation System (ECRES) algorithm against a reference tabular approach to estimate extra carbohydrate requirements for preventing exercise-induced hypoglycemia in 26 adults with type 1 diabetes. The study found that the ECRES algorithm calculated a significantly lower median carbohydrate intake overall compared to the tabular approach (13.5 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), which was particularly marked in physically active participants (9.0 g vs. 23.0 g; P < .01), while both methods successfully prevented hypoglycemia during exercise; post-exercise, ECRES maintained continuous glucose monitoring metrics within recommended target guidelines, whereas the tabular method resulted in significantly higher time below range in the afternoon (11.8% vs. target <4%; P < .05) and time above range during the night (39.3% vs. target <25%; P < .05).
passage_3: Effect of Continuous Glucose Monitoring on Glycemic Control in Adolescents and Young Adults With Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Clinical Trial evaluates the impact of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) compared with standard blood glucose monitoring (BGM) on glycemic control over 26 weeks in 153 adolescents and young adults aged 14 to 24 years with type 1 diabetes. The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.

question: In the study comparing mobile SMBG technology and family-centered goal setting for adolescents with type 1 diabetes, what was the HbA1c reduction at 3 months for the combined approach?
passage_1: Advancing Diabetes Management in Adolescents: Comparative Effectiveness of Mobile Self-Monitoring Blood Glucose Technology and Family-Centered Goal Setting evaluates three strategies—a health information technology (HIT)-enhanced blood glucose meter that shares real-time data and allows text messaging, a clinic-based family-centered goal setting intervention using motivational interviewing, and a combined approach of both—to improve self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) and glycemic control (HbA1c) in adolescents aged 12–18 with type 1 diabetes over a 6-month period. The study found that HIT-enhanced SMBG alone resulted in no change in mean HbA1c, family-centered goal setting showed a non-significant decrease of 0.3% at 6 months, and the combined approach demonstrated a significant HbA1c reduction of 0.6% at 3 months that diminished to a non-significant 0.4% reduction by 6 months, with higher baseline HbA1c levels predicting greater improvement; additionally, there were no significant changes or group differences in the daily frequency of SMBG testing. Based on these findings, the authors recommend further research into pairing family-centered goal setting with HIT-enhanced diabetes technologies, noting that family goal setting and counseling may be particularly useful when adolescents adopt new self-management technologies to achieve optimal clinical outcomes, especially among those with higher baseline HbA1c levels.
passage_2: Family-based Psychoeducation and Care Ambassador Intervention to Improve Glycemic Control in Youth with Type 1 Diabetes: A Randomized Trial evaluates the impact of a 2-year randomized clinical trial testing three levels of care—standard care with basic care coordination, monthly outreach by a Care Ambassador (CA), and monthly CA outreach plus quarterly family-based psychoeducation—on glycemic control (A1C), parental involvement, family conflict, and quality of life among 153 youth with type 1 diabetes. The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Based on these findings, the authors implicitly recommend incorporating structured psychoeducational strategies—focused on teamwork, setting realistic expectations, and joint problem-solving—alongside routine care coordination specifically for youth with suboptimal glycemic control, while cautioning against relying solely on frequent phone or email outreach without targeted behavioral support

Findings demonstrate that structured behavioral approaches—such as skills training, family-based teamwork, behavioral family systems therapy, and multi-systemic therapies—yield modest yet clinically meaningful improvements in regimen adherence, quality of life, and glycemic control, particularly when delivered early post-diagnosis, incorporating family collaboration, or targeting modifiable emotional and family processes rather than relying solely on education. Recommendations highlight tailoring behavioral interventions to meet the unique strengths and needs of individual families, evaluating cost-effectiveness for broader translation, combining mobile and digital health technologies with human contact, and conducting further culturally tailored research for youth with T2D. question: In the cohort sequential study on decision-making involvement in youth with type 1 diabetes, which child-reported subscales peaked around ages 12–14 before declining?
passage_1: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. The study found that median HbA1c peaked in late adolescence at 9.3% for females at age 17 and 9.1% for males at age 19, with overall target HbA1c levels achieved by very few participants (only 11% of adolescents aged 14–17 and 7% of young adults aged 18–25). Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.

Findings indicate that 80% of caregivers and 66% of adolescents logged into a decision aid at least once, spending an average of 55.0 and 46.2 minutes on the website and viewing 72.2% and 77.4% of the content, respectively. Bivariate and regression analyses revealed that non-Hispanic, Caucasian females from higher socioeconomic status households were significantly more likely to log in, while adolescent males with lower health literacy demonstrated fewer logins. Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.

The review found a 22.2% prevalence of depression and a 17.7% prevalence of anxiety among children with type 1 diabetes, with depression being notably higher in girls (29.7%) compared to boys (19.7%) and in lower-middle-income countries (29.3%), while the prevalence of depression among children with type 2 diabetes stood at 22.7%. question: In the SEARCH for Diabetes in Youth Study, what was the prevalence of disordered eating behaviors in youth with type 1 diabetes versus type 2 diabetes receiving insulin therapy?

Analyzing a cohort of 2,156 participants with type 1 diabetes and 149 participants with type 2 diabetes using the Diabetes Eating Problem Survey–Revised (DEPS-R), the study found that DEB was present in 21.2% of individuals with type 1 diabetes and 50.3% of those with type 2 diabetes. question: In the study on early initiation of diabetes devices in children with recent-onset type 1 diabetes, what were the insulin pump and CGM usage rates at baseline and 6-month follow-up?
passage_1: Early Initiation of Diabetes Devices Relates to Improved Glycemic Control in Children with Recent-Onset Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus evaluates whether initiating an insulin pump or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) within the first year of diagnosis is associated with reduced glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels in a cohort of 111 children aged 5 to 9 years with recent-onset type 1 diabetes. Tracking participants from baseline (mean diabetes duration of 4.7 months) to a 6-month follow-up (~12 months post-diagnosis), the study found that insulin pump usage grew from 17% to 35.1% and CGM usage increased from 17.1% to 25.2%. The findings demonstrate that children using an insulin pump maintained lower overall HbA1c levels compared to non-users, and children who started using a CGM during this timeframe experienced significantly lower HbA1c levels than those who did not. Based on these findings, the authors conclude and recommend that early initiation of either an insulin pump or a CGM in newly diagnosed children can help improve glycemic control within their first year of living with type 1 diabetes.
passage_2: The study Treatment regimens and glycaemic outcomes in more than 100 000 children with type 1 diabetes (2013–22): a longitudinal analysis of data from paediatric diabetes registries evaluates temporal trends in HbA1c levels, treatment modalities, and acute complications across international paediatric diabetes registries from 2013 to 2022. Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.
passage_3: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

question: In the Norwegian registry-based longitudinal study, what were the peak median HbA1c levels for females and males during late adolescence, and at what ages?

The authors found that severe hypoglycemia rates per 100 patient-years were 7.1 in T1DX, 3.3 in DPV, and 6.7 in WACDD, and lower HbA1c was not associated with an increased rate of severe hypoglycemia when examined by source registry, treatment regimen, or age group. Based on these findings, the study recommends further investigation in other large, longitudinal cohorts to better characterize the contemporary relationship between glycemic control and severe hypoglycemia risk in pediatric type 1 diabetes patients.
passage_2: The study Hemoglobin A1c Levels and Risk of Severe Hypoglycemia in Children and Young Adults with Type 1 Diabetes from Germany and Austria: A Trend Analysis in a Cohort of 37,539 Patients between 1995 and 2012 evaluates temporal trends in the association between hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels and the risk of severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemic coma in a prospective cohort of 37,539 children and young adults with type 1 diabetes from Germany and Austria between 1995 and 2012. The study found that the relative risk for severe hypoglycemia and coma per 1% HbA1c decrease declined significantly from 1.28 to 1.05 and from 1.39 to 1.01, respectively, over the 18-year period, alongside a continuous increase in daily blood glucose monitoring frequency, short- and long-acting insulin analog use, and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump therapy. Based on these findings, the paper indicates that lower HbA1c levels have become a minor predictor for severe hypoglycemia, allowing clinicians and young patients with type 1 diabetes to aim for near-normal glycemic control to prevent long-term diabetic complications without substantially increasing their risk of severe hypoglycemic events.
passage_3: The study Treatment regimens and glycaemic outcomes in more than 100 000 children with type 1 diabetes (2013–22): a longitudinal analysis of data from paediatric diabetes registries evaluates temporal trends in HbA1c levels, treatment modalities, and acute complications across international paediatric diabetes registries from 2013 to 2022. Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Concurrently, event rates per 100 person-years declined for both severe hypoglycaemia (from 3.0 to 1.7) and diabetic ketoacidosis (from 3.1 to 2.2). Despite these improvements coinciding with increased adoption of diabetes technology, many children still fail to achieve current International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD) glycaemic targets, indicating that further advances in management are required even for youth with access to specialized care and technology.

question: In the SENCE study, what were the effects of CGM combined with a family behavioral intervention versus CGM alone versus standard blood glucose monitoring on time spent in hypoglycemia?

The study found that treatment with CGM resulted in a statistically significant reduction in mean HbA1c levels from 8.9% at baseline to 8.5% at 26 weeks, compared to remaining unchanged at 8.9% in the BGM group (an adjusted between-group difference of -0.37%). Additionally, participants in the CGM group demonstrated improvements in secondary outcomes, including time spent in the target glucose range and reduced daytime and nighttime glucose variability. The study concludes that CGM leads to small but statistically significant improvements in glycemic control in this population and notes that further research is needed to determine the clinical importance and long-term implications of these findings.

question: Across the 20 studies in the systematic review on diabetes family conflict in young people with type 1 diabetes, how many found a significant association between greater family conflict and higher HbA1c values?
passage_1: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.

The findings revealed no overall significant differences in A1C across the three groups at the end of two years, and monthly outreach alone provided no added benefit over standard care when regular quarterly clinic visits were maintained; however, a subgroup analysis of youth with suboptimal baseline control (A1C ≥ 8%) showed that the psychoeducational intervention significantly helped maintain or improve A1C levels (77% vs. 52%) and sustain parent involvement (36% vs. 11%) compared to the combined non-psychoeducation groups, all without increasing diabetes-specific family conflict or decreasing youth quality of life. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

question: In the multiethnic middle-school cohort study comparing hrA1C and IFG, which was more common and which was more persistent over two years?

In this multiethnic 6th-grade cohort of 3,980 students, IFG was five times more common than hrA1C (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but hrA1C was more persistent over a two-year period into 8th grade (59.4% vs. 46.9%). High-risk A1C was strongly associated with non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity, family history of diabetes, higher BMI, waist circumference, and fasting insulin, whereas IFG was associated with Hispanic ethnicity, male sex, higher BMI, waist circumference, fasting insulin, high blood pressure, and mean triglycerides. Over the 2-year study, very few children developed diabetes thresholds (0.8% with hrA1C developed A1C ≥6.5%, and 1.1% with IFG developed FPG ≥126 mg/dL), and only 58% of those identified with diabetes in 8th grade had previous baseline abnormalities. The study notes that optimal screening strategies and guidelines for diabetes in youth remain unresolved due to the modest predictive value of both measures and differing risk profiles.

The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.

question: What percentage of youth with a type 2 diabetes phenotype tested positive for islet autoantibodies (GAD-65 and IA-2) in the study of 1,206 screened participants?

Based on these projections, the paper highlights the urgent need for targeted prevention strategies to attenuate the rising burden of youth diabetes in future decades.

question: Over the 10-year SWEET Project benchmarking period (2008–2018), what were the changes in mean HbA1c, insulin pump use, and CGM sensor use across 22 centers in 19 countries?

question: Does the screening and diagnosis study provide positive predictive value and negative predictive value of HbA1c and FPG for future diabetes development in youth?
passage_1: Screening and Diagnosis of Prediabetes and Diabetes in US Children and Adolescents evaluates the performance of American Diabetes Association risk-based screening criteria and current clinical definitions of prediabetes and diabetes—based on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), or both—to identify high cardiometabolic risk in US youth aged 10 to 19 years. The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.
passage_2: The Diabetes Screening With Hemoglobin A1c Versus Fasting Plasma Glucose in a Multiethnic Middle-School Cohort evaluates middle-school students with glycemic abnormalities by comparing high-risk hemoglobin A1c (hrA1C: 5.7–6.4%) with impaired fasting glucose (IFG: 100–125 mg/dL) to characterize their distribution, durability, and association with other diabetes risk factors. In this multiethnic 6th-grade cohort of 3,980 students, IFG was five times more common than hrA1C (16.0% vs. 3.2%), but hrA1C was more persistent over a two-year period into 8th grade (59.4% vs. 46.9%). High-risk A1C was strongly associated with non-Hispanic Black race/ethnicity, family history of diabetes, higher BMI, waist circumference, and fasting insulin, whereas IFG was associated with Hispanic ethnicity, male sex, higher BMI, waist circumference, fasting insulin, high blood pressure, and mean triglycerides. Over the 2-year study, very few children developed diabetes thresholds (0.8% with hrA1C developed A1C ≥6.5%, and 1.1% with IFG developed FPG ≥126 mg/dL), and only 58% of those identified with diabetes in 8th grade had previous baseline abnormalities. The study notes that optimal screening strategies and guidelines for diabetes in youth remain unresolved due to the modest predictive value of both measures and differing risk profiles.

The authors find that rejecting HbA1c based on lack of correlation with OGTT or FPG is scientifically flawed because neither OGTT nor FPG have themselves been validated against long-term health outcomes (such as retinopathy) in children, and OGTT suffers from low reproducibility. Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.
